newsitem.title: USA: Ford pact heads for vote; Chrysler talks heat up.
newsitem.headline: Ford pact heads for vote; Chrysler talks heat up.

text.p: Ford Motor Co. workers were expected to swiftly ratify a rich new United Auto Workers contract while the union's separate talks with Chrysler Corp. showed signs of progress, officials said Sunday.

Industry observers had expected the UAW, which reached an agreement with Ford earlier this month, to bargain next with Chrysler because the Canadian Auto Workers union is now threatening to strike General Motors Corp.'s Canadian operations.

UAW officials expect Ford workers to approve the pact by an overwhelming margin. The deal provides $13,900 in economic gains for the average worker over the life of the pact, plus substantial increases in pension benefits, and $1,000 per child per year in college tuition assistance.

Meanwhile, senior negotiators from the union have moved their operations into Chrysler headquarters, a company spokeswoman said, while a union source said a new labor deal could be reached as early as Sunday.
"We've been in pretty intensive negotiations at the subcommittee level for the last two days," said Nicole Solomon, a spokeswoman for Chrysler. "We believe we're making progress."
Solomon said it was unclear whether a new labor pact covering the 66,000 UAW workers at Chrysler could be reached Sunday.
She said UAW President Stephen Yokich and Chrysler Chairman Robert Eaton met Saturday afternoon. Other negotiators met past midnight on Saturday.

A source close to the union said UAW officials were "optimistic" an agreement could be reached Sunday. The previous three-year pact between the UAW and Detroit's Big Three automakers, which covers nearly 400,000 workers, expired on Sept. 14.

The UAW and Ford reached a tentative agreement on Sept. 16 that calls for Ford to guarantee employment for 95 percent of its current 105,000 UAW workers over the life of the three-year pact. Final ratification by all of Ford's UAW locals was expected later Sunday.
The UAW extended the deadline for Chrysler and General Motors Corp. A new deadline has not been set, said Solomon.

Industry analysts have said Chrysler could easily afford the provisions of the Ford contract, but that a similar pact could cause problems for GM, which needs to shrink its work force to cut costs to competitive levels.
